raw_text:
**Introduction and Historical Context**
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a rare but life-threatening form of pregnancy-associated heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) [1]. Historically, the condition was first rigorously described by Demakis et al. in 1971, defining it as idiopathic systolic dysfunction presenting in the last month of pregnancy or within five months postpartum [1]. Early clinical studies pointed toward a key role of persistent systemic inflammation and apoptotic pathway activation in its pathophysiology, with significantly elevated plasma levels of cytokines and Fas/Apo-1 seen in affected mothers [2]. While geographic and socio-demographic variations are substantial, the earliest cohort analyses—such as those by Fett et al. in rural Haiti—documented exceptionally high regional prevalence rates, sparking global research into environmental and nutritional cofactors [3]. Comparisons of clinical cohorts in the United States subsequently revealed that women presenting both early and late in the peripartum period shared similar clinical traits, establishing the broader syndrome of pregnancy-associated cardiomyopathy (PACM) [4].

**Pathophysiology: The Two-Hit Model**
The molecular basis of PPCM was historically classified as idiopathic, but basic and translational research over the past two decades has revealed a complex interplay of hormonal, genetic, and vascular factors. In 2007, Hilfiker-Kleiner et al. proposed a groundbreaking prolactin cleavage hypothesis [5]. Specifically, the loss of manganese superoxide dismutase (MnSOD) increases oxidative stress in the peripartum heart, driving cathepsin D to cleave full-length prolactin into a vasculotoxic 16-kDa fragment [5]. This 16-kDa prolactin fragment impairs myocardial angiogenesis, induces endothelial cell apoptosis, and triggers microvascular rarefaction [5]. This hormonal pathway was formally integrated into clinical frameworks through the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) consensus statements [6], which also proposed targeting this path with prolactin-inhibiting bromocriptine therapy [7].

A parallel "hit" involves genetic predisposition. Up to 15–20% of PPCM patients carry pathogenic mutations in genes associated with familial dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) [8]. Specifically, truncating variants of the titin gene (*TTN*) are the most common genetic finding [8]. These genetic predispositions may render the maternal heart vulnerable to the profound hemodynamic and metabolic demands of late gestation [9], occasionally requiring inotropic support such as levosimendan in severe, refractory cases [10].

Furthermore, an intense angiogenic imbalance plays a crucial role. During the late third trimester, the placenta secretes high concentrations of anti-angiogenic factors, particularly soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1) [11]. This anti-angiogenic milieu is strongly exacerbated by multifetal gestations and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, which further starve the maternal microvasculature of vital vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling [11]. Predictive biomarkers for poor outcomes include baseline left ventricular (LV) dimensions [12], low body mass index [12], and elevated levels of asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA) and microRNA-146a—the latter being a direct downstream mediator of 16-kDa prolactin [13,14]. Consequently, there is a profound epidemiological and pathophysiological overlap between pre-eclampsia and PPCM [15], significantly increasing maternal morbidity in affected pregnancies [15].

**Clinical Management and Registries**
Establishing an early diagnosis is critical, particularly because symptoms of PPCM (e.g., dyspnea, edema) mimic the physiologic discomforts of normal pregnancy [16]. Prospective registries in North America (the IPAC study) [17] and genetic studies of cohorts [18] have helped define predictive indicators of myocardial recovery. The American Heart Association (AHA) [19] recommends early initiation of standard heart failure medications tailored to pregnancy and lactation, although renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) inhibitors must be avoided until after delivery [19]. Furthermore, severe LV dysfunction carries a high risk of thromboembolism and sudden cardiac death, requiring early consideration of anticoagulation and wearable cardioverter-defibrillators (WCD) to manage life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias [20].

The addition of bromocriptine to standard heart failure therapy has transitioned from a bench-to-bedside concept to a key component of contemporary PPCM care, as demonstrated in a major multicentre randomized trial [21]. While subsequent pregnancies carry a high risk of relapse [22], preconception counseling and risk stratification by a multidisciplinary "pregnancy heart team" have significantly improved maternal safety, as outlined in the ESC guidelines [23] and clinical reviews [24].

**Global Perspectives and Prognosis**
The modern landscape of PPCM is heavily informed by global registries. Position statements by the Heart Failure Association (HFA) of the ESC have standardized diagnostic thresholds (such as LVEF < 45%) and treatment algorithms [25]. The EURObservational Research Programme (EORP) PPCM registry, enrolling over 700 women from 51 countries, highlighted notable geographic disparities: while recovery rates are high in Europe and North America, maternal mortality remains disproportionately high in regions such as sub-Saharan Africa [26]. Prospective registries from highly prevalent areas like Nigeria (the PEACE registry) further demonstrate the devastating impact of socioeconomic and geographic barriers to timely diagnosis and therapy [27]. Modern clinical recommendations emphasize systematic screening of natriuretic peptides, echocardiography, and genetic counseling for first-degree relatives [28]. Translating these pathophysiological and genetic insights [29] into clinical practice has shifted the prognosis of PPCM from a historically high-mortality diagnosis to a highly treatable condition with high rates of complete myocardial recovery [30].
